html:
The map's label for the early peoples of the Caribbean islands who lived by fishing, gathering shellfish and hunting, shown from 1500 BCE to 1650. Humans first reached Cuba and Hispaniola around 4000 BCE or a little earlier, in what archaeologists call the Archaic age.

The first settlers probably came by canoe from Central America, and others later came up from South America by way of Trinidad. They used stone and shell tools and ate fish, shellfish, sea turtles, manatees and birds. Some also tended useful plants.

From about 500 BCE farming, pottery-making peoples from the Orinoco, called Saladoid, spread up the island chain to Puerto Rico. Their descendants became the Taíno of the larger islands, and the Kalinago later held the smaller islands to the south-east. Older foraging ways lasted on the margins. Spanish writers described a people in western Cuba, the Guanahatabey, who did not farm, though some scholars doubt they were a separate group.

After Columbus arrived in 1492, war, forced labour and disease destroyed most island peoples within a few decades, and Spanish and other European colonists replaced them, opening the Columbian Exchange.
